sections.heading: Appendix 3: Legislation Amendments
sections.text:
The Resources Safety and Health Legislation Amendment Act 2024 amended the CMSHA, to include the following changes below as highlighted in bold italics font. This becomes legislation on 1 June 2025.
Schedule 3 (Dictionary) critical control means a risk control measure for a coal mine -
(a) that is critical to -
(i) prevent a material unwanted event at the coal mine; or
(ii) mitigate the consequences of a material unwanted event at the coal mine; and
(b) the absence or failure of which would significantly increase risk despite the existence of other risk control measures. material unwanted event (MUE), at a coal mine, means an unwanted event in relation to which the potential or real consequence to safety or health exceeds a threshold defined by the coal mine operator as warranting the highest level of attention 30 How is an acceptable level of risk achieved
(2) This Act provides that the systems should incorporate risk management elements and practices appropriate for each coal mine to—
(a) identify, analyse, and assess risk; and
(b) avoid or remove unacceptable risk; and
(c) monitor levels of risk and the adverse consequences of retained residual risk; and
(d) provide for critical controls
(e) investigate and analyse the causes of serious accidents and high potential incidents with a view to preventing their recurrence; and
(f) review the effectiveness of risk control measures, and take appropriate corrective and preventive action; and
(g) mitigate the potential adverse effects arising from residual risk. 47A Obligation of officers of corporations
(1) If a corporation has an obligation under this Act, an officer of the corporation should exercise due diligence to ensure the corporation complies with the obligation.
(2) An officer of a corporation may be convicted or found guilty of an offence under this Act relating to an obligation of the officer whether or not the corporation has been convicted or found guilty of an offence under this Act relating to an obligation of the corporation.
(3) In this section, due diligence includes taking reasonable steps—
(a) to acquire and keep up-to-date knowledge of mine safety and health matters; and
(b) to gain an understanding of the nature of coal mining operations at a coal mine and generally of the hazards, risks and critical controls associated with those operations; and
(c) to ensure the corporation has available for use, and uses, appropriate resources and processes to eliminate or minimise risks to safety and health from work carried out as part of coal mining operations; and
(d) to ensure the corporation has appropriate processes for receiving and considering information regarding incidents, hazards, risks and critical controls and responding in a timely way to that information; and
(e) to ensure the corporation has, and implements, processes for complying with any obligation of the corporation under this Act; and
(f) to verify the provision and use of the resources and processes mentioned in paragraphs
(c) to (e). 62 Safety and health management system
(5) The safety and health management system should be adequate and effective to achieve an acceptable level of risk by—
(a) defining the coal mine operator’s safety and health policy; and
(b) containing a plan to implement the coal mine operator’s safety and health policy; and
(c) stating how the coal mine operator intends to develop the capabilities and support mechanisms necessary to achieve the policy; and
(d) including principal hazard management plans and standard operating procedures; and
(da) identifying critical controls; and
(e) containing a way of—
(i) measuring, monitoring and evaluating the performance of the safety and health management system; and
(ii) taking the action necessary to prevent or correct matters that do not conform with the safety and health management system; and
(f) containing a plan to regularly review and continually improve the safety and health management system so that risk to persons at the coal mine is at an acceptable level; and
(g) if there is a significant change to the coal mining operations of the coal mine— containing a plan to immediately review the safety and health management system so that risk to persons is at an acceptable level. 63 Principal hazard management plan
(1) A principal hazard management plan should—
(a) identify, analyse and assess risk associated with principal hazards; and
(b) include standard operating procedures and other measures to control risk; and
(c) include critical controls

docs.title: Managing welding fume in coal mines

sections.heading: Front matter
sections.text:
E INSPECTORATEL MINE INSPECTORATEQUEENSLAND COAL MINE INSPECTORATE
Queensland Guidance Note QGN36 Managing welding fume in coal mines
Date December 2025 Revision 1.0

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text:
This guidance note provides practical advice for coal mine operators, supervisors and coal mine workers (CMWs) on managing exposure to welding fumes from hot work processes in Queensland coal mines. It aims to provide relevant, practical information specific to Queensland coal mines, without duplicating existing technical guidance.
Information is provided on:
• exposure profiles of CMWs involved in hot work
• common hot work processes and consumables in the coal industry
• risk management principles for identifying, assessing, and controlling exposure
• monitoring methods for evaluating personal exposure risk
• practical strategies for controlling fume
• health surveillance
• educational requirements for CMWs on health effects and control measures
• review and audit.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text:
This guidance note applies to all Queensland coal mining operations under the Coal Mining Safety and Health Act 1999 (Qld) (CMSHA), focusing on controlling and monitoring fumes generated from welding and other hot work activities, where these activities directly involve metals or metal alloys. Processes involving non-metal materials such as vulcanising rubber and plastics including polyethylene pipes are excluded from this guidance note.
For the purpose of this guidance note, hot work includes welding, brazing, soldering, heating, gouging, cutting and grinding, in which the surface temperature of the work, or a tool used for the work, is likely to exceed 150ºC.
This guidance note does not cover the other general safety hazards associated with welding and hot work, including:
• electrocution
• fire and explosion
• burns
• electric shock
• vision damage
• hearing loss including ototoxic effects
• exposure to intense ultraviolet (UV) radiation.
Guidance for managing these hazards should be sourced from other published documents and a list of additional resources including best practices for welding safety, has been provided in Appendix J.
General information only is provided about the toxic gases typically generated from arc welding processes, including ozone (O3). At the time of writing this guidance note, there was limited data available from Queensland coal mines on exposure monitoring results and control effectiveness for these gases. When more data becomes available, this guidance note will be updated.

sections.heading: Legislation
sections.text:
In addition to the objects of the CMSHA, section 6, this guidance note also aligns with Section 42 of CMSHA (State of Queensland 2024), which outlines the site senior executive’s (SSE) obligations in relation to the safety and health of persons who may be affected by coal mining operations. These obligations include ensuring that risks are kept at an acceptable level and the development and implementation of a safety and health management system (SHMS).
Airborne contaminants, such as welding fume, are a health hazard and exposure must be managed at an acceptable level.
Key obligations include:
• Risk Control: Ensuring risks from mining operations are at an acceptable level.
• SHMS Implementation: Developing and implementing a SHMS for all mine personnel, including contractors.
• Training: Ensuring CMWs receive training on hazards and risks related to their work.
• Monitoring: Providing regular monitoring and assessment of the working environment, procedures, equipment and installations.
Additional relevant sections of the Coal Mining Safety and Health Regulation 2017 (Qld) (CMSHR):
• Section 46: Employer must arrange for health assessment o An employer must ensure a health assessment is carried out for each person to be employed or employed, by the employer as a coal mine worker. o The health assessment must be carried out by, or under the supervision of the employer’s appointed medical adviser.
• Section 46A: Content of health assessment o The health assessment must be carried out in accordance with the approved form.
• Section 46B: Other matters to be covered in health assessments o Health assessments may include matters not covered in the health assessment approved form if a risk assessment has been undertaken for a task and where the appointed medical adviser considers the person needs to be assessed to achieve an acceptable level of risk.
• Section 49: Monitoring for workers’ exposure to hazards o The SHMS must provide for periodic monitoring of the level of risk from the hazard. o The SHMS must also provide for the notification of workers, and employers and the employer’s appointed medical adviser of increased risk levels. o Ensuring periodic monitoring of workers’ exposure to hazards.
• Section 96 (a) and (c) (ii): o A coal mine must have a standard operating procedure (SOP) to control access to, and work in, confined spaces at the mine. o A SOP must exist that protects against hazards from cutting and welding, including in confined, wet, or dusty locations.
• Section 102 (A) (c) and 149 (K): o A surface mine and an underground mine must have a principal hazard management plan (PHMP) for airborne dust or any other airborne contaminants.
• Section 263: o Authorisation from the underground mine manager is required for hot work in underground mines, except in permanent underground workshops. The authorisation must be included in the mine record.
This guidance note is designed to assist coal mining operations to satisfy the requirements of CMSHA and CMSHR, in relation to managing welding fume.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text:
Welding is the process of joining two or more metal pieces together by applying intense heat, often with the use of consumable electrodes or filler materials. Welding fumes are generated due to the intense heat and primarily come from the base metals, electrode materials, and any surface contaminants or coatings on the metal being welded (Safework Australia 2024). These fumes consist of airborne particulates, ranging in size from 0.01 to 1 micrometre (μm), with inhalation being the primary exposure route (Australian Institute of Occupational Hygiene 2022). Fumes are also generated from other hot work processes associated with welding, including cutting and gouging.
In addition to particulates, gases such as oxides of nitrogen (NOx), carbon oxides, and ozone (O3) are formed during arc welding.

sections.heading: Health effects from exposure
sections.text:
Inhalation of welding fume and gases is associated with a range of short and long-term health effects that can have serious health consequences (Figure 1). The most significant is the established link between welding fume exposure and lung cancer. Studies indicate that welders have a 30 to 40% higher risk of developing lung cancer compared to the general population and there is a probable association with kidney cancer (Figure 1) (Safe Work Australia n.d., Honaryar MK 2019). Other long-term health effects include occupational lung diseases such as occupational asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, emphysema, bronchitis and siderosis. Acute effects from exposure can also irritate the upper respiratory tract (nose and throat), and result in a flu like response known as metal fume fever and increase the risk of pneumonia.
Other health effects may occur as a result of exposure to specific compounds or metals within the fume. For example, exposures to welding fume containing nickel and chromium, can result in skin irritation or allergic contact dermatitis.
Whilst exposure to welding fume containing lead or manganese may lead to neurological effects. Many metals commonly found within welding fume are known to be ototoxic, including lead and manganese. Ototoxic substances may damage the cochlea (inner ear) and/or the auditory nerve pathways to the brain, leading to hearing loss and tinnitus. The combined effects of exposure, to welding fume and noise can have a synergistic effect, leading to higher levels of hearing impairment, than noise exposure alone. It is recommended that the noise exposure of workers (based on a daily shift) exposed to any ototoxic substances, be reduced below 80 dB(A) (8-hour equivalent) (Safework NSW 2024).
Chronic exposure to ozone may contribute to occupational asthma and may also exacerbate existing respiratory conditions including COPD. All open arc processes will generate ozone gas.
Figure 1: Health effects from exposure to welding fume

sections.heading: Generation of fume/gas from different types of welding and allied hot work processes
sections.text:
The fume cloud consists of particulate from the base metal, welding consumables and any residual surface coatings.
The amount of fume produced, and the composition of the fume cloud will vary depending on the type of welding or hot work conducted, and the composition of consumables and the parent metal.

sections.heading: Welding fume emission
sections.text:
A detailed description of the welding fume composition that is generated by the common welding and hot work methods used in Queensland coal mines, has been provided in Appendix B. These welding methods include:
• Gas metal arc welding (GMAW) • gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW)
• flux-cored arc welding (FCAW) (gas shielded • manual metal arc (MMAW) or stick and self-shielded)
• thermal cutting and gouging
• arc air gouging
• brazing and soldering.
• plasma cutting and gouging

sections.heading: Types and composition of consumables
sections.text: Welding consumables generally contain metals and elements that assist the welding process and protect the weld from the atmosphere. For example, some hard facing consumables often contain high levels of manganese. A list of various types of welding and their composition is included in Appendix D. Further composition detail for each product can be obtained from the consumable’s safety data sheet.

sections.heading: Surface coatings
sections.text:
If a surface coating is present on the material being welded, the welding fume will contain oxides of the metallic coating. For example, a galvanised material will contain high levels of zinc and zinc oxides in the fume generated. In the case of a painted surface, the paint will decompose in the arc and a range of toxic polyaromatic hydrocarbons can be emitted within the welding fume. If the paint is an old lead-based paint, the fume will also contain lead.
In all cases, it is recommended for both personnel safety and weld quality reasons that all surface coatings and contaminants be removed prior to welding. There are various option for removing surface coatings including for example chemical stripping, or mechanical sanding and grinding. Consideration should be given to the secondary exposure risk when selecting a suitable option.

sections.heading: Exposure profile and welding methods used in Queensland coal mines
sections.text:
Most welding in the Queensland coal industry occurs in situ, typically during repairs and maintenance of heavy mobile plant and fixed structures at Coal Handling and Preparation Plants (CHPPs). Welding activities may also be conducted in workshops, confined spaces during plant shutdowns, or underground, though this is less common.
Most coal mines have designated welding bays either as standalone workshops or adjoined to or embedded within other larger workshops, typically used for mobile equipment maintenance. These vary significantly in terms of size, resources and set up. Some sites still have designated bucket shops and undertake significant amounts of intense welding and allied hot works processes in these facilities.
When designated welding areas are being designed consideration should be given to facilitating layout and installation of fixed and portable exhaust ventilation systems and, the separation of welding processes from other activities to minimise secondary exposure.

sections.heading: Boilermaker population and welding practices
sections.text:
A survey conducted by the coal inspectorate between 2022 and 2024 identified that the boilermaker workforce in Queensland's coal mines is approximately 56% full-time employees and 44% contractors (Figure 3). Welding practices differ between these groups, with contractors more likely to weld for longer hours each day, weld for a larger number of days each week and more likely use Metal Inert Gas (MIG) welding (Figure 6), which may result in differing exposure risk profiles.
The majority of welding tasks used on coal mining sites involve mild steel (Figure 4). Other specialty materials such as hard-facing, quench and tempered steels (e.g. bisalloy, weldox, hardox, roqlast or roqtuf), while often applied during the manufacturing of mining equipment, are used to a lesser extent on the mine site. Welding with stainless steel, aluminium and galvanised metal components is relatively uncommon.
FCAW and MIG are the most common welding methods employed, with GTAW (TIG) and stick welding used in more specific circumstances. (Figure 5).

sections.heading: Welding fume exposure
sections.text:
Personal exposure to welding fume is routinely monitored at Queensland coal mines. These samples are collected using inhalable size selective devices positioned in the boilermaker’s breathing zone, although outside of any respiratory protection equipment (RPE), and therefore represent a measure of unprotected exposure. The rates of monitoring have increased significantly over the last 5 to 10 years as awareness of the health risk has been communicated. Samples collected for total welding fume are typically analysed for individual metal components and compared against the relevant Occupational Exposure Limit (OEL) (Safework Australia 2024). A reduction in the OEL for total welding fume from 5 mg/m3 to 1 mg/m3 was introduced by Safe Work Australia (SWA) and came into effect in early 2024.
Currently there is a combination of full shift and task based (episode) monitoring being conducted at coal mines. Full shift personal exposure monitoring conducted on coal mines over the last decade indicates that the current OEL for total welding fume of 1 mg/m has been consistently exceeded. Currently the CMSHA only prescribes a limit for total welding fume in schedule 6: General body concentrations for atmospheric contaminants of 5 mg/m3 This only applies to the underground coal mine environment. There is no limit prescribed for surface coal mines or the surfaces parts of underground coal mines. In these instances, where there is no prescribed limit, the limit published by SWA (Safework Australia 2024) has generally been applied as the default.
Each year Resources Safety Health Queensland (RSHQ) requests coal mines provide records of all personal monitoring for total welding fume, including the individual metal components. RSHQ now holds a dataset comprising of approximately 2,400 valid personal welding fume exposure records. This includes full shift (70% of total) and task based (30% of total) monitoring results with records dating back to 2009.

sections.heading: Risk management process
sections.text:
The potential health effects from welding fume exposure and the level of exposure from the methods typically applied within Queensland coal mines, has been well established in other sections of this guidance note. The primary purpose of conducting a risk assessment within the context of this guidance note, is to identify and rank the potentially exposed workers and SEGs within the mine and determine the level of monitoring and controls to be applied at the mine.
The primary consequence of interest from welding fume exposure in this context are the chronic health effects, including lung disease and in particular lung cancer. The nature of these chronic health effects is such that the risk of harm is related to cumulative exposure over many years and long latency periods, and the symptoms and diagnosis of disease may be 10 to 30 years after exposure. A different approach is required when assessing and ranking these risks, as compared with the methods applied to assess acute safety risks, where the impacts occur at the time of the incident or shortly after. The International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) have proposed a separate Health Risk Assessment (HRA) approach, that includes a number of options to rank risk according to exposure level and this approach has been adopted for reference in this guidance note.
Risk management is a systematic process to eliminate or minimise the potential for harm to people. Regarding welding fume, this process includes the following steps:
• Identify which workers are at risk of exposure to welding fume, including boilermakers and those working in the immediate area.
• Assess the risk using exposure estimates to understand the nature of harm that could be caused, and determine what sources and processes are causing that risk.
• Control risks if it is not reasonably practicable to eliminate risk, implement the most effective control measures that are reasonably practicable in accordance with the hierarchy of controls.
• Review and monitor control measures to ensure they are working as planned.
Figure 9 outlines the risk management process steps applied within this guideline.
Risk assessment must involve appropriate consultation between relevant parties including an occupational hygienist and a cross section of workers, including boilermakers and others potentially affected by welding fume hazards.
Each mine must identify and assess exposure to welding fume as part of the mine operations HRA. As with all other identified hazards, the procedures documented within the mine’s SHMS (e.g. PHMPs, Workplace Risk Assessment and Controls (WRACs), SOPs need to incorporate the outcomes identified in the HRA. The HRA should be reviewed and updated within 5-yearly intervals. Or earlier if there is a significant change to welding practices, exposure, and/or there is a change in the OELs.
A summary of the risk management process is outlined in the flow chart below (Figure 9).
Figure 9: Risk Management Process Steps

sections.heading: Identifying the hazard
sections.text:
The purpose of hazard identification within the context of this guidance is to identify and rank different exposure groups and activities involved with applying hot work methods. The first step in the risk management process is to identify all hazards associated with the welding process. Consideration should be given to identifying the following at the mine site:
• All SEGs engaged in welding tasks and other hot works (RSHQ n.d.).
• All exposed workers within SEGs who may be exposed to welding fume (including boilermakers, firewatchers, trades assistants and others within the immediate working area).
• Welding methods and hot works being conducted.
• Materials and consumables being used.
• Work location and environment (indoors, outdoors, workshops).
• Frequency (i.e. days per week) and duration (hours per day) these hot work methods are applied by each group.
A list of common welding tasks conducted on Queensland coal mine sites is provided in Appendix E.
The hazard identification process should involve the following steps:
• Desktop review of previous HRAs, previous monitoring surveys and exceedance investigations, and safety data sheets.
• Walk through survey - this may include a questionnaire to record specific weld methods, consumable types and controls used by different groups. This should include discussion with boilermakers and supervisors.
• Ranking hazards - this may involve ordering the hot work/welding methods used by each group according to fume emission rates and potential to cause harm. The fume emission rates for different weld methods is summarised in Figure 2. An example of a hazard rating criteria is shown below (Table 1 (ICMM 2016)).The hazard rating for most welding activities where exposures to welding fume are estimated to exceed the OEL and likely cause adverse health effects, will be medium or high, depending on duration/frequency of exposure.
• Recording what welding fume controls are in place and what level in the hierarchy of controls (Figure 10). This should include whether the welding fume controls are being used as intended, if they are being inspected and maintained, and is there a system for monitoring control status and integrity.
Table 1: Example criteria to rate hazards adapted from ICMM Good practice guidance on occupational health risk assessment (ICMM 2016) Hazard Rating Definition 1 – Very Low Exposure is unlikely to lead to harm. (Minor health effects) 2 – Low Non-life-threatening reversible health effects e.g.: irritation to upper (Reversible health effects) respiratory tract, metal fume fever, bronchitis or pneumonia. 3 – Medium Adverse health effects that are permanent but do not significantly affect (Adverse health effects) quality of life or longevity. Health effect that may be mildly limiting or disabling and therefore could lead to a change of occupation and lifestyle. 4 – High Adverse health effects that are generally permanent and could lead to a (Significant and severe significant reduction in quality of life and/or longevity. Continued exposure is health effects) generally likely to lead to permanent physical or mental disability or a longterm limiting illness e.g. kidney or lung cancer.
While the focus of this guidance note relates to the exposure to welding fume, a risk management process should also be applied to the other general safety hazards associated with welding and hot work activities.
Guidance for managing these hazards should be sourced from other published documents and a list of references including best practices for welding safety have been provided Appendix J.

sections.heading: Assessing exposure to welding fume
sections.text:
After completing the hazard identification phase, qualitative and quantitative risk assessment methods should be applied to estimate the incidence and severity of health effects, as a result of workplace exposures. This is then used to develop and prioritise controls and is typically done without considering controls in the first instance. Qualitative and quantitative risk assessment of welding fume should involve consultation with a certified occupational hygienist (COH).
The health effects of interest from welding fume exposure are chronic lung diseases and in particular, lung cancer. The probability should estimate the likelihood of exposure above levels known to cause health effects.

sections.heading: Qualitative risk assessment
sections.text:
Qualitative risk assessment is conducted as a first step to estimate whether exposure is uncertain and further monitoring is required to understand the risk, or if exposure is unacceptable and additional controls are required. This should then be used to inform the broadbrush risk assessment and to identify significant health risks that require more comprehensive measurement and control. This assessment assists in determining:
• the extent of the risk (degree of exposure and potential health effects)
• the effectiveness of current control measures, considering the hierarchy of controls (refer section 8)
• actions to be taken for additional controls and monitoring.

sections.heading: Quantitative risk assessment
sections.text:
Once the qualitative risk assessment has been completed and monitoring conducted to determine the levels of exposures within priority SEGs quantitative risk assessment should be used on an ongoing basis to determine the levels of risk, effectiveness of controls and priorities for further control investigation. An example of quantitative exposure rating criteria is shown below in Table 2.
Semi-quantitative risk assessment should be completed for any SEG groups that are not included in the list of priority SEGs selected for minimum exposure monitoring requirements (Table 4). This requires professional judgement to estimate the relative exposure level for each SEG that has not been monitored, by comparing the frequency and duration of hot work activities, and weld methods with those SEGs that have been monitored. (EN 689 2019)

sections.heading: Risk acceptability
sections.text:
If the average exposure for a SEG is above the OEL, then the risk is deemed to be unacceptable, and further controls should be implemented. In addition, when considering risk acceptability, controls should be implemented to ensure the exposure risk is controlled to as low as reasonably achievable. This includes the application of higher order controls before considering any protection provided by RPE.
When assessing risk, the statutory exposure limits prescribed for airborne contaminants within the CMSHR legislation, shall be applied in the first instance. In the absence of statutory limits being prescribed for specific airborne contaminants, the OEL values published by Safework Australia should be applied.

sections.heading: Controlling the risk
sections.text:
Controls implemented to manage welding fume exposure should follow the hierarchy of controls. This should consider eliminating or minimising the level of fume by focusing on the process first, followed by ventilation and finally RPE. In most cases a combination of controls will be required in order to achieve an acceptable level of risk.
A detailed list of practical welding fume controls that follow the control hierarchy and which are available for use in the coal mining industry, have been outlined in Section 0 and are summarised in Appendix E.

sections.heading: Review and verification of control effectiveness
sections.text:
To ensure welding fume exposure remains effectively controlled, the risk management process should incorporate a documented process to (i) validate the effectiveness of new controls introduced; (ii) periodically review the effectiveness of existing welding fume controls; and (iii) include a process for routine in-shift validation of existing control performance.
(i) The effectiveness of new controls can be validated by taking measurements before and after new fume controls are introduced at the mine, either by using gravimetric or real time sampling methods. Alternatively, the results of validation measurements reported from other sites, or published by supplier/manufacturer groups or by research studies, for the same control type, may be used for reference.
(ii) Periodically reviewing the effectiveness of existing welding fume controls should include an annual review of the exposure monitoring results from the mine, maintenance inspection reports completed on fume control equipment, and any incident reports in relation weld fume control devices.
(iii) Routine in-shift validation of fume control performance should include in-shift inspection and monitoring the operating condition of the device and comparing this with design parameters. For example, this may include direct measurement or checking display gauge readings for pressure, flow rate, or air velocity.
(iv) Manufacturers of fume controls should facilitate in-shift performance validation, by installing monitoring and display systems onto the equipment, or by providing measurement tools, to confirm design parameters are being maintained during equipment operation. For example a flow or pressure gauge mounted onto a fixed exhaust ventilation system to indicate the system is functioning as intended.

sections.heading: Audit and review
sections.text:
A review of the risk assessment should be conducted when controls fail to reduce exposure to an acceptable level, before any workplace or process changes, when new hazards are identified, when consultation with CMWs or other stakeholders highlight the need for review, or at the request of a Site Safety and Health Representative.
An audit and review of procedures documented within the mine’s SHMS, in relation to the monitoring and control of welding fume, should be conducted periodically to ensure ongoing effectiveness and continuous improvement, and exposure to welding fume are being managed to an acceptable level of risk.

sections.heading: Change management
sections.text:
The change management process should be triggered when there is a proposed change to the type of hot work and welding methods, consumable types and/or materials being welded, at the mine. The change management process should identify the potential impacts on welding fume exposure and the potential introduction of new hazards and risks.
Before new control measures are applied to manage exposure to weld fume, a change management process should be applied, to ensure the introduction of any new risks are identified and managed effectively. For example, a poorly controlled fume ventilation system may disturb the gas shield around the molten metal pool, resulting in reduced weld integrity.

sections.heading: Personal monitoring for welding fume exposure
sections.text:
The monitoring of welding fume exposure should be generally aligned to the concepts and requirements for monitoring respirable dust, as specified in Recognised Standard 14: Monitoring respirable dust in coal mines
(RS14).
Where there are unique requirements for monitoring welding fume these are outlined in the guidance below.
Where welding fume has been identified in the mine’s PHMP for airborne contaminants, this should include requirements for a welding fume personal exposure monitoring program.

sections.heading: SEGs
sections.text:
The SEGs relevant to welding activities at each mine must be established and used to develop the mine’s welding fume monitoring program.
The list of SEGs applied to the monitoring and reporting of sampling results for respirable coal dust in accordance with RS14, do not adequately define the smaller exposure groups of CMWs performing welding activities.
Therefore, a separate list of SEGs that perform common welding activities and which contribute to the majority of welding fume exposure, within coal mining have been included in Table 3. For the purpose of reporting welding fume exposure monitoring data to RSHQ, all data should be assigned to the SEGs listed in Table 3.
These are unique to welding activities and there is currently no requirement to monitor these SEGs for other airborne contaminants such as respirable dust and respirable crystalline silica.
The separate SEGs that perform welding activities have unique exposures not experienced by other workers and were identified from a review of industry data and surveys conducted in the development of this guidance note. It was also identified that some work groups with elevated exposure to welding fume were not being monitored. For example, historical monitoring for welding fume was typically focused on boilermakers performing intermittent breakdown repairs from the mobile equipment workshop, whereas more frequent and longer duration welding exposures were being experienced by groups of CMWs doing refurbishment and shutdown work on heavy mobile equipment (HME), and these were not being monitored.
Notwithstanding the requirements to use SEGs listed in Table 3 for reporting purposes, mines should establish and use their own SEGs based on observations and the exposure profile of their specific work groups, and cover the activities listed below:
• Plant maintenance; o heavy mobile equipment maintenance o infrastructure maintenance (e.g. buildings, conveyors, run-of-mine (ROM) bins) o coal processing plant maintenance.
• Maintenance locations; o workshop based o field based.
• Maintenance type; o breakdown o routine minor plant shutdown o major plant shutdown/overhaul o refurbishment projects (e.g. buckets, truck trays).

sections.heading: Minimum sampling requirements
sections.text:
The review of industry data and surveys conducted in the development of this guidance note, has confirmed that weld fume exposure in Queensland coal mines is characterised by a relatively consistent and limited range of weld methods, materials, and consumables. The primary difference in exposure risk between groups of CMWs, is the frequency and duration of fume generating activities. This can be broadly separated into two exposure categories:
• Prolonged welding periods (e.g. > 6 hours), typically scheduled in advance (e.g. HME plant maintenance shutdowns).
• Intermittent welding periods (e.g. ≤1–2 hours), typically unscheduled (e.g. HME plant breakdowns).

sections.heading: Minimum samples and frequency of monitoring
sections.text:
An exposure monitoring plan has been developed to characterise welding fume exposures to workers within the Queensland coal mining industry (Table 4).
This minimum sampling plan has been developed to effectively sample and characterise the exposure profiles of a limited number of selected SEGs. These SEGs represent the range of potential welding fume exposures from both prolonged and intermittent welding categories and most common welding tasks applied within Queensland coal mines.
The number of samples specified for each SEG is the minimum number required to support simple statistical analysis to estimate the exposure for that group (S.M and Selvin 1987).
A COH or equivalent should develop and endorse the monitoring program and conduct annual reviews of the program.

sections.heading: Limitations with minimum sampling plan
sections.text:
This minimum sampling approach has been chosen solely for estimating welding fume exposure for the purpose of this guidance note. The minimum sampling numbers have been applied so as not to compromise the sampling capacity already committed to the previously established monitoring programs for other airborne contaminants, including but not limited to respirable dust and crystalline silica.
As a consequence of this approach, there are a number of limitations inherent within the minimum sampling plan and these should be considered when interpreting the results of monitoring over time.
Limitations with minimum sampling plan include:
• Exposure monitoring for welding fume is inherently biased in that sampling is typically only conducted when welding activities are being performed and do not include periods or shifts when there is no exposure. Consequently, the result of this sampling only provides an estimate of exposure intensity during welding activities and this may overestimate the actual long-term exposure.
• Full-shift sampling is used for groups engaged in prolonged fume-generating activities. These results can be compared directly with OELs. Cross-contamination can occur from airborne contaminants generated by non-welding tasks that occur during the sampling period.
• Task-based sampling is used where exposures are intermittent and short duration. While it reduces cross-contamination uncertainty, the sample period may not be representative of exposure over the whole shift and therefore introduces worst-case sample bias. These results cannot be directly compared with OELs without applying professional judgement and having comprehensive knowledge about what exposures occurred during portions of the shift that were not monitored.
• Focusing sampling on a limited number of welding SEGs improves the reliability of estimating exposure for the groups being monitored. This approach does not sample all welding SEGs and estimating the exposure for these groups will require qualitative analysis using extrapolation. This will result in limited data to assess the effectiveness of controls being applied by these groups.
• The limited numbers of samples for each welding SEG collected each year, may result in variable results, and this should be considered when interpreting results and estimating welding SEG exposure.
The review of exposure data over a greater period than one year may be required where fewer than six samples have been collected.
• While priority should be given to monitoring the welding SEG specified in Table 4, adjustments may need to be made for some mines where the population of boilermakers and/or allocation of welding work, does not align with these groups. For example: o For small mines where welding tasks may be infrequent and insufficient to be allocated into the specified welding SEG, monitoring for welding fume should be conducted on welding groups applicable to the mine. o For large mines where the welding SEG listed in Table 4 do not adequately cover the range of welding tasks and potential exposures at the mine, additional sampling should be conducted to characterise the exposure profile of these other groups and/or larger populations of exposed CMWs. o Additional welding SEG may be monitored at the discretion of the mine site, and this could be a requirement resulting from risk assessments, investigations or concerns raised by CMWs.

sections.heading: Personal exposure sampling
sections.text: Sampling should be scheduled with maintenance planners and coordinators to ensure plant shutdowns and other project work is included in the monitoring plan. Sampling should primarily focus on welding tasks where practical, although other hot work tasks directly associated with welding may be included. Workers should be randomly selected for each sampling period to minimise sampling bias and samples should be representative of exposure to welding fume.

sections.heading: Competency requirements
sections.text:
The competencies required to develop exposure sampling plans and conduct personal exposure sampling should align with the requirements applied for respirable dust in section 4.3 of RS14. In addition, a person who is developing sampling plans and conducting personal exposure sampling for welding fume, should have familiarity with this guidance note, and the following:
• welding methods
• potential sources of sample contamination/damage/invalid samples
• welding fume controls
• safety hazards associated with welding and hot works.

sections.heading: Sampling methods
sections.text:
Personal exposure sampling Samples must be collected from the breathing zone in accordance with the standard sampling method (ISO 10882-1:2024). For the purpose of assessing exposure within the context of this guidance note, sampling heads should be positioned in ambient air behind face shields but outside any respiratory protection. For example, given that Powered Air-Purifying Respirator (PAPR) provides both respiratory protection and incorporates the face shield, the sampling head must be placed in the breathing zone outside the PAPR helmet.
Where the boilermaker is wearing a face shield (that does not incorporate a respirator) the sampler must be positioned in the breathing zone behind the face shield. The sampler may be positioned and attached to the inside of the face shield. Alternatively, the sampler may be positioned outside and behind the face shield, by attaching the sampler high up onto the wearer’s shirt collar.
In both cases the sampler must be orientated in accordance with manufacturer instructions, to ensure the size selective sampling of airborne exposure concentrations is conducted effectively.
The position of the sampler must be recorded on the field sheet and accompany the reporting of results.
The sampler may be positioned in other locations within the breathing zone for the purpose of verifying control effectiveness and not assessing exposure.
The total duration of all welding tasks and the type of welding method, across the full shift period, must be recorded on the field sheet (Appendix C). (EN 689 2019)

sections.heading: Task-based sampling
sections.text: Samples should be collected only during welding fume generation activities. Multiple periods may be combined into a composite sample. All welding tasks conducted during the shift should be sampled. The sampling of nonwelding activities should be minimised to avoid contamination and these recorded where they occur. A minimum runtime of 50 minutes per sample is recommended unless shorter durations are justified by highexposure tasks.

sections.heading: Full-shift sampling
sections.text: Samples should cover at least 80% of the shift. This may include all types of hot work activities conducted during the shift.

sections.heading: Sampling equipment
sections.text:
Size selective sampling devices should be used to sample personal exposure to welding fume for comparison with the OEL. These devices must be certified by an accredited third party to conform with the standards for the relevant size fraction sampling convention (EN 481-1993) (BS EN 481 1993) (BS EN 13205-1,2:2014) (ISO 7709-1995 (ISO 2023)).
Equipment used to sample welding fume must be fit for purpose and maintained to achieve the objectives stated in the relevant sampling standards AS3640/AS2985 and this guidance note. Sampling equipment must be subjected to periodic calibration and performance checking, at least annually. _______ This runtime has been established based on the calculation in clause 9.1.3.1 of ISO 10882-1 (ISO 10882-1:2024 2024), using a limit of reporting of 0.01 mg/m for undifferentiated welding fume in the inhalable fraction.

sections.heading: Standard for collecting and analysing welding fume samples
sections.text:
All samples collected for the purpose of personal exposure assessment should be collected and analysed in accordance with ISO 10882-1:2024 (ISO 10882-1:2024 2024). Laboratories performing analysis of welding fume samples must be accredited by the National Association of Testing Authorities (NATA) to Australian Standards (AS) ISO/IEC17025:2018 general requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories for the gravimetric determination of inhalable dust and respirable dust (AS ISO/IEC 17025:2018 International Organization for Standardization 2018 ). Analysis for welding fume metals must be in accordance with a standard method. All analytical results reported by the laboratory for personal exposure sampling, should include the uncertainty in the reported results.
As a minimum, the following sampling and analysis should be conducted:
• total welding fume (inhalable fraction)
• metal suite analysis (inhalable fraction).To include the following recommended minimum metals: o Iron Oxide Fume (Fe), Manganese Fume (Mn), Nickel Metal (Ni), Total Chromium (Cr), Copper Fume (Cu), Zinc Oxide Fume (Zn).
Additional sampling and analysis should be conducted where other contaminants are identified and likely to contribute to an exposure risk, including but not limited to:
• Manganese (respirable fraction) – if the manganese (inhalable fraction) exceeds 50% of the shift adjusted OEL, consider additional sampling the respirable fraction.
• Hexavalent Chromium (inhalable fraction) - if the total chromium (inhalable fraction) exceeds 50% of the shift adjusted OEL, consider additional sampling for Hexavalent Chromium.
• Other contaminants, where these are considered likely to contribute to exposure based on the consumable and welding technique (refer Appendix D).
Analysis for total welding fume and metals should be in accordance with a recognised method. Examples include but are not limited to the following:
• Total welding fume - Gravimetric analysis to determine the total inhalable fraction mass of welding fume according to AS 3640.
• Metal suite analysis - Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) or mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) is used after acid digestion of the filter media according to NIOSH 7300, 7301, 7303, or ISO 15202. X-ray fluorescence (XRF) may also be used.
• Respirable manganese - Gravimetric analysis to determine the respirable fraction mass of welding fume according to AS 2985, with manganese analysis included in the metal suite analysis.
• Hexavalent Chromium – Analysis of fume collected onto filter media using ion chromatography and UV detection according to OSHA ID-215 (version 2) (Occupational Safety and Health Administration n.d.).

sections.heading: Invalidating samples
sections.text: Personal exposure samples that do not meet relevant method for the sampling and analysis of welding fume and metals are invalid and must not be used for estimating exposure. The criteria for which samples are classified as invalid should be in accordance with section 7.9 of RS14.

sections.heading: Limit of reporting and censored data
sections.text: Personal exposure sample results that are reported as below the laboratory limit of reporting are referred to as censored data or non-detects and treatment of these should follow the requirements outlined in Section 7.4 of RS14.

sections.heading: Tampering with samples or results
sections.text:
A person must not tamper, or allow another person to tamper, with a sample or the results of a sample taken to monitor a worker’s exposure to welding fume at a coal mine. This is further outlined in section 10 of RS14.
Sampling records Records of personal exposure sampling performed for welding fume must be kept for 30 years at the coal mine and follow the requirements outlined in section 7.8.3 of RS14. Observations of the welding task(s) performed and controls used during the monitoring period(s) should be recorded with sample records. The minimum information to be recorded for each sample is outlined in Appendix C.

sections.heading: Other monitoring methods
sections.text: There are a range of other monitoring methods, that can be used to identify sources of exposure and assess control effectiveness, as outlined in sections 6.2, 6.3 and 6.4 of RS14.

sections.heading: Investigating exposure exceedances
sections.text:
If a single personal full shift exposure sample result, exceeds the relevant shift adjusted exposure limit, an investigation should be initiated. The investigation should determine the absent or failed control/s that contributed to the measured exposure, and identify the actions required (short and/or long term) to ensure welding fume exposure is as low as reasonably practicable. Reference should be made to the range of welding fume control options listed for common welding methods in Appendix E.
At a minimum, the investigation should consider the following:
• date of sample • environmental location (indoors, outdoors, confined space)
• SEG
• operators head position (inside plume, outside
• work location plume)
• crew
• adjacent activities contributing to exposure
• activities/tasks carried out (including on-arc (other welding tasks in close proximity) times, weld method, and other hot work
• maintenance schedule vs actual maintenance tasks performed). records for all equipment (e.g. PAPR, on-tool,
• Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) used welding equipment, extraction) and for what activities/tasks (including
• equipment pre-start checks/status of welding times). fume controls
• controls in place. Refer to control options
• sampling data (determine if sample valid) listed in Appendix E.
• operational conditions (e.g.
• base metal consumables (e.g. mild steel, normal/maintenance, shift/downtime). consider coatings)
• environmental wind conditions (still, light breeze, windy) The results of the investigation should be recorded and analysed in conjunction with previous investigation findings, to identify any trends and changes required with the coal mine’s SHMS. Any subsequent changes made to the SHMS must also be recorded and communicated to affected CMWs.

sections.heading: Reporting
sections.text: Communication of personal exposure results At the end of each sampling period, personal exposure sample results should be communicated to individual CMWs that participated in the monitoring and de-identified results made available to all CMWs at the mine, regardless of the measured concentration.

sections.heading: Annual sampling result
sections.text: Individual mines will be requested by RSHQ at the end of each calendar year, to forward the results of personal exposure sampling for welding fume. Sampling records including SEG results should be submitted to RSHQ in the approved format provided.

sections.heading: Assessment of exposure risk
sections.text:
Estimating SEG exposure Assessment of exposure risk for individual SEGs should be conducted by a COH or equivalent.
For the purpose of this guidance, the exposure profile for each SEG should be estimated separately and compared with the OEL to determine if the exposure is acceptable, unacceptable or uncertain.
• Where monitoring data is available for the SEG, the exposure should be calculated using quantitative analysis. This includes welding SEGs identified for minimum sampling requirements (Table 4) and/or other groups monitored at the mine.
• Where monitoring data is not available, the exposure for this welding SEG should be estimated using semi quantitative analysis, by comparing with similar groups and activities that have been monitored and using professional judgement. This includes work groups not listed for minimum sampling requirements (Table 4). (EN 689 2019) Following the collection of sufficient samples, inferential statistics should be generated to summarise the dataset and estimate the exposure profile for the SEG. Various tools can be used to generate descriptive statistics, as outlined in RS14. This includes the free industrial hygiene statistical excel tool from the American Industrial Hygiene Association (AIHA n.d.).
To assess and determine if risk is acceptable the analysis should calculate the average exposure concentration for the welder workgroup and SEG (6.1.2). Professional judgement may be required, due to inherent variability of welding fume exposure concentrations and should include consideration of the following:
• average (mean/Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimate (MVUE))
• measures of variability Geometric Standard Deviation (GSD)
• confidence intervals (95% upper confidence limit)
• range (min-max).
These will determine whether further sampling is required.
Where task based sample data is being analysed consideration should be given to welding activities performed during the shift and whether the sampling is representative of all welding fume exposure in the shift. Where task based sampling is not representative, the analysis of this data can only be used for qualitative assessment.
Additional methods to assess exposure may include:
• reasonable worst-case measurements (maximum exposures likely to occur with controls in place)
• estimating exposure (using appropriate models or algorithms)
• comparison with other similar operations and welding activities.
When qualitative methods for assessing exposure are inadequate to estimate exposure, additional sampling is recommended. (EN 689 2019)

sections.heading: Monitoring program review
sections.text:
Site should review their welding fume monitoring program on an annual basis and submit their review to the SSE.
If there are significant changes to the plant, equipment, operating environment, operating methods, or SEGs that have the potential to impact welding fume exposure levels, or there is a significant change to the exposure estimate following periodic monitoring, the frequency of sampling must be reviewed.

sections.heading: Hierarchy of controls
sections.text:
Elimination will require the need to completely remove the hazard from the workplace by replacing it with alternatives – There are limited examples of practical ways to eliminate the need for hot work and welding required in coal mining.
Replacing/substituting either the base metal or the welding type/technique to reduce exposure.
Examples include substituting FCAW with MIG, SS FCAW and GS FCAW.
Engineering design to reduce exposure with the use of equipment, tools and design.
Examples include robotic welding, on tool extraction, local exhaust ventilation (fume capture hoods).
Administrative procedures, documents and training that assist in control effectiveness to reduce exposure.
Examples include adequate maintenance schedule and pre-checks, worker rotation, worker positioning and training packages.
Personal protective equipment to reduce exposure to welding fume.
Examples include the correct selection, use and maintenance of respiratory protection with focus on the use of PAPR.
Figure 10: Hierarchy of Control as applies to welding fume (British Occupational Hygiene Society n.d.) To achieve an acceptable level of risk and minimise exposures to welding fume to as low as reasonably achievable, the selection of control measures to reduce welding fume, should follow the hierarchy of controls with higher order control measures considered first.
In practice the management of welding fume will require a combination of different order controls to be applied, to be effective.
A summary of the fume control options available for common welding tasks performed in Queensland coal mines has been tabulated in Appendix E.

sections.heading: Elimination
sections.text: Alternative methods such as mechanical/chemical joining techniques, that eliminate the need for hot work and welding are not suitable for the types of repair work required in coal mining and are outside the scope of this guidance note. Should more information become available on suitable alternatives, this guidance note will be updated.

sections.heading: Substitution or modification of process
sections.text:
Substituting or modifying the welding process can reduce the welding fume emission rate and potential for exposure. A change management process should always be conducted to ensure the quality and standard of weld specified by the manufacturer of the plant being repaired, is not compromised. In some cases, the alternative process will have to be trialled and validated, for the manufacturer to authorise the change.
There are a large range of alternative options available for selection, to reduce the generation and concentration of airborne welding fume during welding.

sections.heading: Welding method
sections.text:
The emission rate of welding fume is primarily determined by the welding method used, as summarised in
Figure 2. Where feasible, selecting lower fume-emitting welding processes can significantly reduce airborne fume concentrations. For example, opting for a GMAW process such as MIG with solid wire, instead of FCAW, or choosing gas-shielded FCAW over gasless FCAW for the same task, can substantially reduce the volume of welding fume generated.
However, these substitutions may require additional skill and tighter weld procedure control to maintain weld integrity. For instance, when replacing FCAW with MIG, weld quality can be maintained using waveform control and targeted training to improve the welder’s technique.
Process-specific considerations include:
• FCAW remains appropriate for welding in the field or where the welding location cannot be effectively shielded from wind.
• Solid wire MIG is suitable for repairs and allows for faster welding, provided the operator uses spray transfer or pulsed mode. Note that the shielding gas composition, particularly those with high CO₂ content may limit the ability to run in these modes.
• Solid wire MIG in spray mode produces approximately one-third the fume of FCAW under comparable conditions.
• Caution should be exercised when attempting deep single-pass welds (e.g. 8 mm) with MIG, as this can lead to metallurgical issues such as centreline cracking. Mines may not be aware of these risks if weld procedures have not been appropriately qualified.
• New generation plasma gouging equipment can produce significantly less fume than traditional air arc gouging for certain applications, specifically those involving the removal of small volumes of weld material with relatively shallow penetration requirements.

sections.heading: Welding machine
sections.text:
The use of modern inverter-based welding power sources, especially synergic pulse power sources, is known to enhance arc stability compared with the use of older transformer-based power sources. Maximising the stability of the welding arc is essential to minimising excess weld spatter, and this is known to reduce welding fume. This can also be achieved by optimisation of weld procedures, and ensuring that the welding torch, cables and electrical connections are well maintained.
Waveform-control technologies commonly utilised in both pulsed spray mode and controlled short circuiting
(dip) mode for the solid wire GMAW process for example, permits welding at lower average amperages and voltages than would be otherwise possible whilst maintaining good control and stability of the process, including productivity and arc penetration characteristics. Use of pulsed spray mode can reduce welding fume produced by up to 80%.
Waveform controls are not effective on the FCAW process other than where metal-cored wires are utilised.

sections.heading: Shielding gas
sections.text:
Shielding gas primarily comprised of a mixture of inert gas typically Argon (Ar) generates less welding fume compared with active gas which is predominantly comprised of Carbon Dioxide (CO2).
Where possible, for gas shielded welding process, select a shielding gas with low CO2 content. Replacing an Ar/18%CO2 shielding gas mix with an Ar/10%CO2 mix can reduce the volume of welding fume evolved by up to 50% (Emily Quecke 2023). This option is effective for both the GMAW and FCAW process (including metal cored wire). When substituting shielding gas, consideration should be given to the manufacturers’ recommendations for specific consumables.
Consumable electrodes and wires classified for use with an Ar/10% CO2 (Standards Australia 2022) shielding gas mix should be selected.

sections.heading: Electrode/wire composition
sections.text:
There are a range of consumable electrodes and wires with compositions designed to minimise the fume generation rate and toxicity of fume generated. For example:
• for the GMAW and FCAW processes, copper-free wire consumables are available, that have been confirmed to generate less fume than copper coated wires
• new low-Mn seamless FCAW wires are available to minimise Mn emissions
• chromium free wires are available as an alternative consumable wire for use in hard facing processes.

sections.heading: Isolation/separation
sections.text: Remotely controlled and operated welding equipment removes the boilermaker from the location where the welding process is applied and from where the welding fume and gases are being generated.

sections.heading: Robotic welding
sections.text:
Robotic welding provides one option for remote controlled welding, allowing the workers to operate the equipment from a safe distance or even from separate control rooms. This not only reduces the risk of inhalation of welding fume and gases but also limits exposure to other welding-related hazards, such as intense UV radiation and heat. Robotic welding systems can be equipped with a variety of welding processes, including MIG and TIG to accommodate different materials and joint types.
There are two primary categories of robots:
• Cobots, or collaborative robots, are designed to work alongside human operators in a shared workspace and can also be operated remotely. They are typically smaller, more flexible, and equipped with advanced sensors and safety features that allow them to detect and avoid harmful contact with humans. Cobots are particularly useful in applications requiring frequent adjustments or a high degree of human-robot interaction. The smaller portable size enables them to be relocated to weld applications in situ, which is an advantage for large mining equipment shutdowns including draglines.
• Industrial robots, are larger, more powerful machines designed for high-speed, high-volume production environments. They are ideal for repetitive, high-volume welding operations. The larger fixed application of these robots has limited application on coal mine sites, where large welding jobs are typically performed outside the workshop and in the field.
Robotic welders bring significant advantages, including improved weld quality, reduced material waste, and enhanced worker safety. The increased weld capacity has the potential to introduce additional exposure hazards which require additional controls to be implemented. For example, the increased weld rate/temperature may generate higher welding fume concentration and the additional weld material deposited, requires an increase in grinding performed by the boilermaker each shift.
There is one coal mine site in Queensland that has commenced trialling the use of cobot welding for dragline shutdowns. This trial has successfully demonstrated the cobots effectiveness at completing welding activities, particularly in applications and positions which are less suitable for humans. These include welding over prolonged durations in awkward positions and inside confined spaces.
Figure 11 and Figure 12 show the trial cobot welder setup in various locations on a dragline shutdown.
Figure 11: Shows cobot with boilermaker performing weld Figure 12: Shows cobot with boilermaker performing weld repairs on a dragline. repairs on a dragline.

sections.heading: Submerged arc welding
sections.text: Submerged arc welding is a process that creates an arc under a bed of flux thereby containing the evolution and emission of welding fume into the surrounding air. It is mainly used in the manufacture of large components of mining equipment, before reaching the mine site. There is limited application of submerged arc welding on the mine site where hot work is primarily directed at repair type welding, often in situ.

sections.heading: Types of ventilation
sections.text:
Static ventilation In static wind conditions welding fume tends to rise upwards and disperse due to its thermal buoyancy. It gradually cools and reaches thermal equilibrium with the surrounding air, after which it falls back down.
Maximum fume concentration occurs at the weld source and often between the weld source and the boilermakers head during most conventional manual welding practices. The concentration naturally decreases with distance away from the weld as the fume rises and disperses.

sections.heading: Natural ventilation
sections.text:
Natural ventilation in the mining context typically refers to the wind conditions which are present in the absence of any mechanical ventilation system. Natural ventilation occurs in the outdoor environment, or as flow through ventilation passing through buildings and workshops which are opened to the external wind conditions, through roller doors, windows and louvers. To a lesser extent natural ventilation can occur inside buildings as the result of temperature differences causing convection flow resulting in an up draft toward the roof (AS/NZS 4740 2000). Roof extraction fans may need to be used to supplement the natural air flows generated by convection currents.
In general, natural ventilation is unreliable and not effective at reducing the fume concentration at source or in the area around the boilermaker’s head and breathing zone, during conventional welding practices. At sufficient wind speeds, natural ventilation can provide sufficient air flow to displace and blow the fume away from the boilermaker’s head and breathing zone, if the boilermaker is positioned upstream of the wind direction. Most of the welding in coal mining is performed outside in natural ventilation.
To minimise exposure to welding fume in natural ventilation conditions the boilermaker must deliberately position themselves and their head away from the fume cloud.

sections.heading: General ventilation (mechanical ventilation)
sections.text:
General ventilation is also known as mechanical ventilation in mining and refers to the supply and exhaust of air from an area or room, using mechanical fan ventilation systems. Fans are used to control the direction, quantity and rate of air flow to a designated location. Fans should not be positioned to direct welding fume towards other workers. Welding screens can be used to assist with controlling the direction of air flow.
Where possible, separate welding bays and/or designated welding workshops should be established and segregated from other workshop areas to prevent welding fume contamination and secondary exposure risks for other CMWs.

sections.heading: Dilution ventilation
sections.text:
Dilution ventilation occurs where positive air flow containing uncontaminated air is introduced to the plume to further disperse and reduce the fume or gas concentration.
Exhaust ventilation Exhaust ventilation is where negative pressure air flow is introduced to capture and remove the airborne contaminants. There are a range of different exhaust ventilation systems available to control welding fume and suited to different applications. Each type has advantages and disadvantages depending on the practical application. The closer the extraction point is to the weld the more effective at controlling the fume generated (Figure 13).
Figure 13: Exhaust ventilation and the proximity to the weld source results in more effective fume capture (European Welding Association 2024).

sections.heading: Local exhaust ventilation (LEV)
sections.text:
Local Exhaust Ventilation is where the extraction is positioned to capture the fume at source before it reaches the breathing zone. The two types of exhaust ventilation commonly used in practice and considered in this guidance note are the on-tool (on-torch) and welding fume hood.
The use of other ventilation systems for welding fume control including fixed welding booths, welding bench enclosures/hoods, and general/displacement ventilation exhaust fans applied to buildings, are not considered practical for the typical welding applications in coal mining, which are generally outdoors and conducted in situ on large fixed or mobile plant.
Capture velocity is the minimum air flow rate required by the exhaust ventilation to capture and remove the welding fume and is typically 0.5-1m/s.
These fume extraction systems are typically (not always) fitted with particulate filtration media to capture the collected welding fume before it is discharge to atmosphere. The filter media should be rated/labelled as High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) class filtration. The fixed systems typically have higher capacity filtration systems and require less frequent replacement compared with the smaller portable units. Consideration should be given to controlling the potential risk of secondary exposure during cleaning and replacement of filtration systems.

sections.heading: On-tool exhaust (form of LEV)
sections.text:
The modern on-tool exhaust system has fully integrated local exhaust ventilation into the hand piece and has the capture vents positioned to provide a suitable capture velocity where the fume is generated, while minimising the risk of removing shield gas and compromising weld integrity. The exhaust ventilation is typically provided by a vacuum system which is separate to the weld machine/shield gas and is either a stand-alone portable system or can be plumbed into an existing fixed extraction system.
The performance and effectiveness of on-tool fume exhaust systems depends on a number of factors including technique, positioning, orientation (angle) and direction. For example, fume exhaust works best using down hand position and is least effective when vertical or overhead. Numerous studies have been conducted to estimate the effectiveness of fume reduction from using on-tool exhaust systems (Knott, et al. 2023). It is estimated the fume reduction will range between 50 and 95 percent (Knott, et al. 2023).
There are a range of on-tool exhaust systems commercially available in Australia for most FCAW, MIG and limited TIG applications. These include fixed or portable systems. A comparison of modern on-tool hand pieces and traditional units are shown in Figure 14 and Figure 15. The weight of on-tool exhaust handpieces are heavier than conventional units, due to the extra exhaust tubing. They can be up to 0.5 kilograms heavier compared with conventional units. This accounts for the trailing cables/exhaust tubing and is measured at a height of 1.5 metres above the ground.
There are a number of coal mines where boilermakers are using on-tool exhaust for routine welding jobs, including both fixed systems inside the workshop and portable systems outside in the field (Figure 16 and

sections.heading: Fume extraction hoods
sections.text:
Fume extraction hoods are completely independent of the weld equipment and are designed with adequate flow rate to provide sufficient capture velocity to entrain and capture the fume away from the boilermakers breathing zone.
The effective capture distance out from the extraction hood is specified by the manufacturer for each device and for a standard 150 millimetres and 200 millimetres diameter hood this is typically 300 millimetres and 450 millimetres, respectively. To be effective the distance between the hood and the weld must be within the capture distance of the hood, and in practice this is approximately one to two diameters. The capture distance is also influenced by the positioning of the extraction hood relative to the weld. For standard hoods this is typically positioned vertically and directly above the weld in the direction of thermal up lift, or on the bench as shown in Figure 18. Placing the hood horizontal and in contact with the bench has the effect of extending the hood. Some modern designs include a flat edge on one side of the hood to facilitate placement onto the bench top for this purpose. Placing the hood at 45 degrees to the weld is the least effective position (Figure 19).
Figure 18: Hood positioned Figure 19: Hood positioned at 45 Figure 20: Hood positioned adjacent directly above the weld. degree angle to the weld. to weld piece.
The performance and effectiveness of fume extraction hoods primarily depends on the positioning of the hood in relation to the weld and this requires the boilermaker to continuously adjust and maintain optimal hood positioning while performing the weld. In practice the optimal hood position is typically not able to be maintained consistently for situations where the boilermaker moves location.
The capture efficiency from fume hoods is also susceptible to cross wind which interferes with the capture velocity. It is estimated from laboratory studies that the fume reduction when hoods are in the optimal position with no cross draught and welding in one location, will be up to 80 percent. Simulated in-field testing in workshop conditions has indicated the fume capture efficiency was approximately 90 percent (Knott, et al. 2023). Optimal performance is rarely achieved in practice in coal mining where the boilermaker does not weld in the one location and there are always cross drafts present.
Fume extraction hoods are commercially available in a large range of fixed and portable configurations and can include single or multiple hoods connected to the same system.
Fume hoods are not limited to the type of weld method or consumable being used as is the on-tool exhaust system and hoods can be utilised in a large range of indoor and outdoor scenarios.
